client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to focus on anything. Every time I sit down to study, my mind drifts back to him and I end up just staring at the wall for an hour. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me actually get through these exams, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is genuinely heavy — grief doesn't pause for deadlines, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to your grandfather when you try to sit down and study. I notice there's a lot of pressure in how you're speaking, and even some doubt about whether this can help, which tells me you're pushing yourself hard while also feeling quite lost right now. Let's take this one step at a time together — acknowledging your grief doesn't have to compete with preparing for your exams, and we can work on gentle strategies that honor both.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I guess I'm not sure how you can "honor both" when they feel completely at odds with each other. Like, if I let myself actually feel the grief, I'm scared I'll just fall apart completely and never open a textbook. And if I push the grief aside to study, I feel guilty, like I'm somehow disrespecting his memory by trying to move on so fast.
therapist: The tension and urgency in your voice really comes through, and what you're describing is such a painful double bind — like every choice feels like a betrayal of something important. But I want to gently challenge the thought that feeling grief means you'll "fall apart completely," because that's actually a prediction your mind is making, not a fact — many people find that allowing small, contained moments of grief can actually *free up* mental space rather than consume it. Honoring your grandfather's memory and preparing for your future aren't opposites; in fact, he likely wanted good things for that future too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about it being a prediction, and maybe you're right, but it doesn't feel like just a prediction, it feels very real and certain to me. And the part about him wanting good things for my future, I don't know, it's a nice thought but it also feels a little too neat, like something people just say to make you feel better. What I keep getting stuck on is what "small, contained moments of grief" even looks like in practice, because I genuinely don't know how to feel something and then just... stop.
therapist: You're right to push back on the "neat" framing — that was too tidy, and you deserve honesty over comfort. The way you're speaking, quickly and with real intensity, tells me this isn't abstract for you; you're genuinely wrestling with this right now, not just talking about it. A "contained moment" might look something like setting a 10-minute timer, looking at a photo of him or writing one thing you miss, and then gently — not forcefully — returning to your work, with the understanding that the grief isn't being abandoned, just paused until you can give it more space.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The timer idea is interesting and I hadn't thought about it that way, but I'm worried that when the 10 minutes is up I won't actually be able to pull myself back out. Like, what if I look at his photo and it just opens something up that I can't close again, and then I've lost the whole evening right before an exam? I think part of me would almost rather just keep avoiding it entirely than risk that happening.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with a kind of tightness to it — tells me this fear feels very live and urgent right now, not hypothetical. That fear of "opening something you can't close" is worth taking seriously, and it's actually a signal that avoidance has been working as a short-term coping strategy, which makes complete sense given how much pain is underneath. But I'd gently ask: has avoiding it fully actually been giving you that focus and safety you're hoping for, or has it been costing you something too — like those hours staring at the wall?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: No, if I'm being honest, the avoidance isn't really working either, because those hours staring at the wall are basically happening anyway. So I guess I'm stuck in this place where neither option feels safe, and that's actually kind of exhausting to admit out loud. I just don't know how to trust that I can handle whatever comes up if I do let myself go there, even for ten minutes.
therapist: That took real courage to admit, and I can hear in your voice — there's a kind of worn-down honesty there, like you've been holding this exhausting tension for a while and it's finally coming out. What you just said is actually really important: you've identified that avoidance isn't protecting you the way you hoped, which means part of you already knows that staying stuck isn't the answer either. The question of whether you can *handle* what comes up is worth sitting with — because you've already been handling grief, stress, and uncertainty every single day for weeks, even imperfectly, and that's evidence of more resilience than you're giving yourself credit for right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that, the resilience thing, but it's hard not to hear it as another one of those things therapists say to make you feel better about yourself. Like, surviving something and actually handling it well feel like really different things to me, and I'm not sure staring at walls and feeling guilty counts as handling it. But I guess... I don't know, maybe there's something small in what you're saying, even if I can't fully accept it yet.
therapist: The way you're speaking — loud, fast, with a kind of urgency — tells me there's real energy behind that pushback, even as your words are reaching toward something small and tentative at the end. You're right to distinguish between surviving and handling things well, and I won't flatten that difference — but I'd ask you to notice what you just did in this conversation: you challenged me when something felt hollow, you were honest about the avoidance not working, and you stayed open enough to find even a small thread of something useful. That *is* handling something, even if it doesn't look the way you imagined it should.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That's actually... harder to dismiss than I expected, and I'm sitting here trying to find the flaw in it but I can't quite. I think part of me has been so focused on what I'm not doing right that I hadn't noticed I was doing anything at all. I'm still not sure it's enough to get me through next week, but maybe that's a separate question from whether I can handle ten minutes with a photo of him.
therapist: There's something really significant happening right now — your words are finding a kind of quiet clarity, but your voice is still racing and stretched tight, like part of you is both relieved and a little unsettled by what you just realized. That separation you just made — between "can I handle ten minutes" and "will it be enough to get me through everything" — is genuinely good CBT thinking, breaking an overwhelming question into something smaller and more testable. You don't have to solve next week tonight; you just have to find out what ten minutes actually feels like, and that's a much more manageable experiment than the one your mind has been running.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, "experiment" is actually a word I can work with more than "exercise" or "homework," because it takes some of the pressure off getting it right. I think my biggest remaining fear is doing it alone, like, what if I try the ten minutes tonight and it goes badly and there's nobody there. But I also know I can't exactly call someone at midnight just because I looked at a photo and got overwhelmed, so maybe I need to think about what a backup plan would look like.
therapist: Your voice still carries that high, quick energy — like you're thinking through this in real time, which tells me you're genuinely problem-solving now rather than just worrying, and that's a meaningful shift. The fact that you're already thinking about a backup plan before you even try the experiment shows real self-awareness — so let's build that plan: it might look like writing down one or two grounding steps you'd take if it feels like too much, like putting the photo away, making tea, or texting someone a simple "thinking of you" without needing to explain everything. You don't have to be alone with it in the sense of being without a plan — having that safety net ready is part of what makes the experiment feel survivable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The backup plan idea actually makes the experiment feel less like walking off a cliff, which I didn't expect. I think I could manage putting the photo away and making tea, those feel like concrete enough things that I could actually do them instead of just freezing up. I'm still a little nervous about trying it tonight specifically, with the exams so close, but I think if I keep waiting for the "right time" that's probably just avoidance wearing a different outfit.
therapist: There's still a lot of tension in your voice — fast, loud, pitched high — even as your words are landing in a much steadier place, which makes sense because insight and nervous system don't always catch up to each other at the same pace. But what you just said at the end is one of the sharpest things you've said all conversation: recognizing avoidance in disguise is genuinely hard to do, and you did it yourself without me pointing it out. You have a plan, you have a backup, and you have more self-knowledge walking out of this conversation than you came in with — that's not nothing, especially the night before a week like this one.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I came in here pretty skeptical that talking would actually change anything practical, and I'm a little surprised to find that I don't feel quite as stuck as I did an hour ago. I think I'm going to try the ten minutes tonight, maybe after I eat something, because you're right that waiting for perfect conditions is just another way of not doing it. I'm still scared, but it feels more like a manageable scared than a paralyzed scared, if that distinction makes any sense.
therapist: That distinction makes complete sense, and it actually captures something important — "manageable scared" means you're moving toward something rather than being frozen by it, which is a real shift from where you started. Your voice has settled into something steadier and more measured than it was earlier, even if there's still some nervousness there, and I think that reflects what you're describing. You came in skeptical and you're leaving with a plan, a backup, and a little more trust in yourself — go eat something, and then let yourself have those ten minutes with him.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
